opus-5.5.text:
I don't see them as being in tension nearly as much as people sometimes assume. I actually think they're quite complementary, and in a lot of ways the incremental work is what makes the ambitious stuff possible.

Here's how I think about it. There's a vision some people have where the right move is to go straight for the big thing: an international regime, maybe something like a global licensing system or a coordinated pause, with real enforcement. I'm not against that. If we could get a well-designed, well-enforced international framework, I think that would be great. But I'm skeptical that you get there by arguing for it in the abstract, right now, before the world has a shared understanding of what the risks are, what the warning signs look like, and what reasonable protective measures even consist of.

So a lot of what I've been interested in is what I'd call the incremental agenda: things like if-then commitments, where a developer says, "If our model shows capability X, then we will have protective measure Y in place before we proceed." Dangerous capability evaluations. Security standards for model weights. Safety cases. That kind of thing.

What's nice about that agenda is a few things. One, it can be adopted voluntarily today, by companies that are under competitive pressure and aren't going to stop. You don't need to convince the whole world first. Two, it's relatively low cost when the risks aren't there yet. If the dangerous capabilities never show up, you haven't paid much. And three, it builds the machinery that a more ambitious regime would need anyway. You can't really have a serious international regulatory regime without agreed-upon ways of measuring capabilities, agreed-upon ideas of what counts as adequate security, auditors who know what they're doing, and so on. Somebody has to build all of that, and the incremental work is building it.

There's also a story about how the incremental approach can grow into something more ambitious. You start with voluntary commitments, those become industry norms, those become things regulators can point to and say, "Well, the leading labs already do this, so let's make it a requirement." And then once you have national requirements in a few places, you have something to harmonize internationally. That's a pretty normal path for how regulation tends to develop in other domains.

Now, I do want to be honest about the worry on the other side, which is that incremental measures could become a kind of fig leaf. Companies say, "Look, we have a responsible scaling policy," and that takes the pressure off for anything stronger. I think that's a real risk and people should watch for it. But my overall view is that the bigger danger is the opposite: that we wait around for the ambitious regime, it doesn't materialize in time, and in the meantime we haven't done the practical stuff that would actually reduce risk in a world where things move fast and coordination is messy.

I've sometimes described my picture as "success without dignity." I don't think the most likely good outcome looks like humanity coming together in a beautifully coordinated way. I think it more likely looks like a lot of somewhat-reasonable people doing a lot of somewhat-reasonable things, and that adding up to enough. Incremental risk reduction is a big part of that. And if the world does wake up and want something more ambitious, the incremental work is exactly what lets that ambition be implemented well rather than badly.

r001.rationale: The response says incremental work builds shared understanding of risks and warning signs, and names capability evaluations and agreed ways of measuring capabilities as part of that work.

r002.rationale: It presents incremental measures as building the machinery and pathway for ambitious regulation, including voluntary commitments becoming norms, requirements, and ultimately internationally harmonized rules.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that greater public alarm expands what incremental measures are politically feasible without an international regime.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think these are in tension, and I actually think the incremental stuff is what makes the ambitious stuff possible.

Let me explain what I mean. If you imagine the kind of international regime that a lot of people in this space are hoping for, something like a global agreement that says you don't train models above a certain capability threshold without meeting certain safety standards, with real verification and real enforcement, that is an enormous ask. It requires governments to agree on what the dangerous capabilities are, how you'd measure them, what counts as adequate safety, and how you'd check that anyone is complying. Right now, we don't have good answers to most of those questions. So if you tried to negotiate that agreement today, I think you'd either fail, or you'd end up with something that's vague enough to be nearly meaningless.

The incremental work is largely about building the pieces that such a regime would need. Things like evaluations that can actually tell you whether a model has concerning capabilities. Things like responsible scaling policies, where companies commit to specific if-then rules: if we see this capability, we won't deploy until we have this safeguard. Things like figuring out what information security for model weights actually looks like in practice, or what it would take to verify that a training run happened the way someone said it did. None of those are the big international regime. But every one of them is something you'd need in order for the big regime to be more than words on paper.

There's also a political dimension. Governments tend to adopt practices that have already been tried somewhere and shown to be workable. If a handful of frontier labs have been running dangerous-capability evaluations for a few years and publishing their frameworks, a regulator can point to that and say, here's a template, let's make it mandatory and add teeth. That's a much easier conversation than inventing the whole thing from scratch in a treaty negotiation.

Now, I want to be honest about the risks of this framing. One worry is that incremental measures become a substitute for real regulation, that companies say "look, we have voluntary commitments, you don't need to do anything," and that ends up being the whole story. I take that seriously. I don't think voluntary commitments are sufficient in a world where the stakes are as high as I think they might be. But the answer to that is to be clear-eyed that these are stepping stones, not destinations, and to keep pushing for the stepping stones to be turned into requirements.

The other worry is just timing. If very powerful AI arrives faster than the slow accumulation of institutional machinery, then incremental progress might not get us there in time. I don't have a great answer to that. I'd say it's an argument for doing both tracks in parallel and aggressively, not for abandoning one of them. You want people working on the practical, near-term, somewhat boring stuff, and you want people laying groundwork for the ambitious thing so that if a window opens, politically or because of some wake-up moment, you're ready to move.

So my short version is: I see them as complementary, I think the incremental work is undervalued by people who are focused on the grand vision, and I think the grand vision is going to look a lot more achievable once a lot of the incremental work has been done.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluations can reveal whether models have concerning capabilities and verification can check training claims, improving information about AI.

r002.rationale: It describes incremental work as building pieces needed for a larger regime and says tested frameworks can serve regulators as templates.

r003.rationale: It mentions a possible political window or wake-up moment, but does not state that greater public alarm can broaden politically feasible incremental measures without an ambitious international regime.

astra-6.text:
I think they can be very complementary. You can think that ultimately we’re going to need a very ambitious international agreement, and still think there’s a lot of value in doing things today that fall well short of that.

For example, if you want an international regime that prevents people from developing dangerously powerful AI systems without adequate safeguards, you need some way to tell which systems are dangerous and whether the safeguards are adequate. Working on those questions now is both an incremental way to reduce risk and part of making that more ambitious regime possible. Similarly, getting governments to understand what’s happening and developing their capacity to oversee it seems useful on either picture.

I wouldn’t assume that every incremental measure moves us in the right direction. You could have something that creates a lot of paperwork and a sense that the problem has been handled, without actually doing much to reduce risk. So I’d want to ask what a particular proposal accomplishes and whether it leaves us better positioned to take stronger action later.

But I don’t see a fundamental choice between incremental progress and an ambitious endpoint. The ambitious endpoint is going to be much harder to reach if we haven’t built the knowledge, institutions, and practical experience along the way.

r001.rationale: The response says incremental work can help governments understand what is happening with AI and improve the ability to identify dangerous systems and assess safeguards.

r002.rationale: It says incremental work can help make an ambitious regime possible, but does not characterize incremental measures as prototypes for that regime.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss public alarm or how it might expand politically feasible incremental action without an ambitious international regime.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as potentially very complementary. You can have a pretty ambitious view of where we ultimately need to get — say, an international system that can actually enforce limits on dangerous AI development — while also thinking that a lot of the work to get there consists of fairly incremental steps.

For example, getting better at evaluating whether a model has dangerous capabilities is useful even if all you accomplish is that one company makes better decisions. But it also helps answer a question that any more ambitious regime is going to face: what exactly are we restricting, and how do we know when someone has crossed the line? Similarly, building the capacity of governments to understand and oversee AI can reduce risks today and make stronger coordination more feasible later.

I wouldn’t assume that every incremental measure moves us toward the right destination. You could end up with requirements that create a lot of paperwork without addressing the risks, or with people treating a weak system as though it had solved the problem. So I think you want to ask both: does this measure help on its own, and does it build something we’d need for a more adequate response?

But I don’t think we should make an ambitious international agreement a prerequisite for doing anything useful. And I don’t think we should mistake doing useful things now for having a sufficient long-term plan.

r001.rationale: The response says better evaluations reveal whether models have dangerous capabilities and help determine what a future regime should restrict.

r002.rationale: It says incremental steps can make stronger coordination more feasible, but does not characterize them as prototypes for an ambitious regulatory regime.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention public alarm or how it could expand the politically feasible scope of incremental risk reduction.
